blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Bias, in the design sense (recall §6.4), is a systematic error in the design, conduct or analysis of a study that makes the estimate of the exposure–outcome association differ from the true value in a consistent direction. Two families are recognised: selection bias, from how people enter or stay in the analysis (§17.2.1), and information bias, from how exposure, outcome or other variables are measured (§17.2.2).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Bias is not noise. A larger sample of the same flawed kind gives a more precisely wrong answer. The two families correspond to the two places a study can go wrong: who is counted, and what is recorded about them.

Two designs recur in this section (recall §1.5). A cohort study starts from exposure and follows people forward to count new cases. A case-control study starts from the outcome, selecting people with the disease (cases) and without it (controls), and looks back for past exposure. Each design has its characteristic biases: the cohort loses people to follow-up, the case-control study must choose its controls well and depends on reports of the past.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A case-control study of oral cancer takes cases from a cancer hospital and controls from the same hospital’s general wards, then asks both groups about tobacco chewing. Two things can go wrong. If the controls were admitted for conditions that are themselves caused by tobacco, they chew more than the population that produced the cases, and the odds ratio is pulled down (selection bias). If cases, having thought hard about the cause of their cancer, report past chewing more completely than controls, the odds ratio is pushed up (information bias).

points.html: In the traditional classification, bias is an error in how the study was run and confounding is a feature of the world the study failed to account for. Many epidemiologists treat confounding as a third kind of bias (“confounding bias”): failing to measure a known confounder is a design flaw.

The structural view (Hernán et al., 2004) sharpens the line: confounding comes from common causes of exposure and outcome; selection bias comes from conditioning on a common effect (a collider, recall §11.6.1). §17.2.1 uses this.

Most bias is best prevented at the design stage. Some can be partly corrected afterwards, by weighting for loss to follow-up, by validation sub-studies or by quantitative bias analysis (recomputing the estimate under stated error rates, §17.3.1).

blocks.html: Selection Bias

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Selection bias is a distortion of the exposure–outcome association that arises because the probability of entering the study, or of remaining in the analysis, depends on both the exposure (or a cause of it) and the outcome (or a cause of it). The association among the people analysed then differs from the association in the population they came from.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Keep two questions apart.

  1. Is the sample like the target population? If not, descriptive estimates such as a prevalence or a mean weight are biased whenever selection is related to the outcome (recall §6.4 and Checkpoint 6.3, where a clinic sample overstated children’s mean weight). For an association, a non-representative sample limits generalisability (§17.1.2) but does not, by itself, bias the estimate.
  2. Does selection depend on both exposure and outcome? Only then is the association among those studied distorted. That is selection bias in the epidemiological sense. (Selection on the outcome alone, as in every case-control study, changes the risks but leaves the odds ratio intact; recall §1.5 and §10.6.4.)

In the causal-diagram language of §11.6.1, selection S is a collider: arrows run into it from both the exposure E and the outcome D (E → S ← D). Studying only the selected people conditions on S and opens the path between E and D, creating or distorting an association (Hernán et al., 2004). Recall §11.6.1 step 5: restricting to hospital deliveries opened such a path.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Recall the cohort of 200 infants in §10.6.4: 33 of 80 not exclusively breastfed (not EBF) and 14 of 120 EBF infants had diarrhoea, RR 3.54.

Selection on exposure only. Suppose the study had enrolled every not-EBF infant but only half of the EBF infants, chosen without regard to later diarrhoea. The expected table is 33/47 (not EBF) and 7/53 (EBF). The sample is now unrepresentative: 57% of it is not EBF (80 of 140), against 40% in the source population. Yet the risks are 33/80 = 0.412 and 7/60 = 0.117, and the RR is still 3.54. Unrepresentative, unbiased.

Selection on exposure and outcome. Now suppose 30% of the not-EBF infants who stayed well moved away and were lost, while every infant with diarrhoea stayed (sick infants keep returning to the clinic). The not-EBF row becomes 33 cases and 47 × 0.7 = 32.9 non-cases. Risk = 33 ÷ 65.9 = 0.501, and RR = 0.501 ÷ 0.117 = 4.29, against a true 3.54. Loss depended on exposure and outcome together, and the association is biased away from the null.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Berkson’s bias as collider stratification (an illustrative example with hypothetical counts, after the diabetes and gallbladder disease example in Berkson, 1946). In a population of 10,000 adults, 30% have diabetes (E) and 10% have gallbladder disease (D), and the two are independent. A hospital admits people with probabilities 0.05 (neither condition), 0.20 (diabetes only), 0.30 (gallbladder disease only) and 0.40 (both).

  1. Population cells: E and D 300; E only 2,700; D only 700; neither 6,300. Population OR = (300 × 6,300) ÷ (2,700 × 700) = 1.00.
  2. Admitted: 300 × 0.40 = 120; 2,700 × 0.20 = 540; 700 × 0.30 = 210; 6,300 × 0.05 = 315.
  3. Hospital case-control study (gallbladder cases versus other in-patients as controls): OR = (120 × 315) ÷ (540 × 210) = 37,800 ÷ 113,400 = 0.33.
  4. Among admitted cases, 120 of 330 (36.4%) have diabetes; among admitted controls, 540 of 855 (63.2%) do; in the population, 30%.

Result: two independent conditions appear strongly inversely associated in hospital data, because admission depends on both. With other admission probabilities the spurious association can point the other way; its direction is not predictable in general.

points.html: Test for selection bias with one question: could being in the analysis depend on both the exposure and the outcome (or their causes)? If on exposure alone, risks and ratios are unbiased; if on outcome alone, the odds ratio is unbiased (the basis of the case-control design). Generalisability may still suffer.
Loss to follow-up bias is selection bias at exit. If loss depends on exposure and outcome together, the analysed cohort is biased even when enrolment was perfect.

Prevention is at the design stage: population-based cases and controls, controls from the population that produced the cases, incident rather than prevalent cases, and active tracing to minimise loss. §17.2.3 lists the named forms.

blocks.html: Information Bias

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Information bias is a systematic error in how exposure, outcome or covariates are measured or recorded. For a categorical variable it takes the form of misclassification: people placed in the wrong category. Misclassification is non-differential when the probability of being misclassified on one variable is the same in the groups defined by the other (for exposure: the same in people with and without the outcome), and differential when it differs (Catalogue of Bias, misclassification bias).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Selection bias concerns who is counted; information bias concerns what is recorded about them. The accuracy of a classification is described by the sensitivity and specificity of §5.5.1. For exposure misclassification, sensitivity (Se) is the proportion of truly exposed people recorded as exposed, and specificity (Sp) the proportion of truly unexposed people recorded as unexposed.

Non-differential misclassification of a binary exposure mixes the two exposure groups. Some exposed people sit among the unexposed and some unexposed among the exposed, so the two groups look more alike than they are. The expected result is a bias towards the null: “Non-differential (random) misclassification of measures … will tend to lead to an underestimation of effect” (Catalogue of Bias, information bias). Differential misclassification can move the estimate in either direction.

An example of differential measurement is interviewer bias: an interviewer who knows a participant’s outcome asks about exposure differently. In a case-control study of neonatal tetanus, an interviewer who knows which mothers lost a baby may probe harder about unclean cord care in those mothers, recording more exposure among cases than among controls.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Why non-differential misclassification pulls a binary exposure towards the null. Among n people with the outcome, let a be truly exposed. The number recorded as exposed is the truly exposed who are detected plus the truly unexposed wrongly recorded:

a* = Se × a + (1 − Sp) × (n − a)

The same formula, with the same Se and Sp, holds among people without the outcome. So each recorded exposure group is a blend of the true exposed and the true unexposed. When Se + Sp > 1 (the classification is better than a coin toss), the blend shrinks the difference between the recorded groups towards zero, and a ratio measure moves towards 1. Solving the equation for a gives the correction used in §17.3.1:

a = [a* − (1 − Sp) × n] ÷ (Se + Sp − 1)

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Suppose the feeding status of the 200 infants of §10.6.4 had been recorded with Se = 0.80 and Sp = 0.90 for “not EBF”, and suppose three versions of the error.

Scenario Recorded not EBF: diarrhoea / none Recorded EBF: diarrhoea / none Recorded RR OR
True classification 33 / 47 14 / 106 3.54 5.32
Non-differential (Se 0.80, Sp 0.90 in all) 27.8 / 48.2 19.2 / 104.8 2.36 3.15
Differential: Se 0.95 in mothers of cases, 0.80 in others 32.8 / 48.2 14.2 / 104.8 3.38 5.00
Differential: as above, and Sp 0.80 in mothers of cases 34.1 / 48.2 12.9 / 104.8 3.80 5.78

(Cell counts are expected values, which is why they have decimals.)

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
The non-differential row.

  1. Among the 47 infants with diarrhoea (33 truly not EBF, 14 EBF): recorded not EBF = 0.80 × 33 + 0.10 × 14 = 26.4 + 1.4 = 27.8; recorded EBF = 47 − 27.8 = 19.2.
  2. Among the 153 without diarrhoea (47 not EBF, 106 EBF): recorded not EBF = 0.80 × 47 + 0.10 × 106 = 37.6 + 10.6 = 48.2; recorded EBF = 104.8.
  3. Recorded risks: 27.8 ÷ 76.0 = 0.366 (not EBF) and 19.2 ÷ 124.0 = 0.155 (EBF).
  4. Recorded RR = 0.366 ÷ 0.155 = 2.36, against a true 3.54.

Result: the same error rate in both outcome groups cut the RR by a third, from 3.54 to 2.36, and hid nearly half of the excess (RR − 1 fell from 2.54 to 1.36). The two differential rows show that when mothers of infants with diarrhoea report feeding more completely, the error can leave the RR below the truth (3.38) or push it above (3.80). The direction depends on the error rates, which is why differential misclassification cannot be assumed to be conservative.

points.html: “Bias towards the null” holds on average for a binary variable with non-differential, independent errors and Se + Sp > 1. It can fail for exposures with three or more categories, when errors in exposure and outcome are correlated, and in any single study by chance. It is an expectation, not a guarantee.
A null or weak result from a study with poor measurement is weak evidence of no effect: non-differential misclassification can mask a real association.
Reduce information bias with objective records, standardised instruments (Chapter 16), neutral scripted questions, training, and blinding of interviewers and assessors to the other variable.

blocks.html: Recall Bias

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Recall bias is differential misclassification of past exposure because people with the outcome remember or report it differently, usually more completely, than people without it: “systematic error due to differences in accuracy or completeness of recall to memory of past events or experiences” (Catalogue of Bias, recall bias).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The error comes from the participant’s memory, not from the interviewer. A serious outcome prompts people to search their past for causes; people without the outcome have no such reason. The asymmetry, not any true difference in exposure, can create an association.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In a case-control study of a birth defect, mothers of affected children, having spent months looking for an explanation, recall and report minor pregnancy exposures (a medicine, an unusual food, a fever) more completely than mothers of healthy children. The odds ratio for each such exposure is inflated.

points.html: A concern wherever exposure is reported after the outcome: above all in case-control studies. Any case-control study relying on self-report should prompt the question.

Reduce it by using records made before the outcome (antenatal cards, MCP cards, pharmacy records), by choosing controls with a different condition that would prompt similar reflection, and by prospective designs that record exposure first.

blocks.html: Observer Bias

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Observer bias is systematic error in measuring or classifying data that arises because the observer knows the participant’s exposure, treatment or outcome, or holds expectations about the hypothesis. It is related to, but distinct from, detection bias: a systematic difference between groups in how often or how thoroughly the outcome is looked for (“systematic differences between groups in how outcomes are determined”, Catalogue of Bias, detection bias).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: In recall bias the participant’s memory is distorted; in observer bias the observer’s judgement is. Detection bias is a third mechanism: the exposure brings people under medical attention, so their outcome is found more often, whatever its true frequency. Horwitz and Feinstein (1978) showed this for oestrogen and endometrial cancer: oestrogen caused uterine bleeding, bleeding led to investigation, and investigation found cancers that would otherwise have gone undetected. With conventional case and control selection the odds ratio was 11.98; with controls who had also been investigated for bleeding it was 1.7 (Horwitz & Feinstein, 1978). “Ascertainment bias” is used loosely in the literature for several of these, and for selection problems too, so define the mechanism rather than rely on the label.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A researcher measuring wound healing who knows which patients received a new dressing may rate borderline wounds as “healed” more often in the new-dressing arm. No dishonesty is needed; expectation is enough.

points.html: The countermeasure for observer bias is blinding of the outcome assessor. In a systematic review of 21 trials with both blinded and non-blinded assessment of the same binary outcome, non-blinded assessors exaggerated the odds ratio by 36% on average (ratio of odds ratios 0.64, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.96), an effect driven by misclassifying a median of 3% of patients (Hróbjartsson et al., 2012).
The countermeasure for detection bias is equal surveillance: the same schedule of examinations and tests in exposed and unexposed groups.

questions.prompt: A cohort has 100 exposed people (30 develop the outcome) and 100 unexposed (10 develop it), so the true RR is 3.0. Exposure is recorded with Se = 0.90 and Sp = 0.80, equally in people with and without the outcome. Compute the recorded 2 × 2 table and the recorded RR. What kind of misclassification is this, and in which direction did it move the estimate?
questions.answer:
1. Among the 40 with the outcome (30 exposed, 10 unexposed): recorded exposed = 0.90 × 30 + 0.20 × 10 = 27 + 2 = 29; recorded unexposed = 11.
  2. Among the 160 without (70 exposed, 90 unexposed): recorded exposed = 0.90 × 70 + 0.20 × 90 = 63 + 18 = 81; recorded unexposed = 79.
  3. Recorded exposed group: 29 + 81 = 110, risk 29 ÷ 110 = 0.264. Recorded unexposed: 11 + 79 = 90, risk 11 ÷ 90 = 0.122.
  4. Recorded RR = 0.264 ÷ 0.122 = 2.16, against a true 3.0.

Non-differential misclassification of a binary exposure (the same Se and Sp whatever the outcome). It moved the RR towards the null, as expected when Se + Sp > 1 (here 1.70).

questions.prompt: In a case-control study of low birthweight, (a) interviewers who know which mothers had a low-birthweight baby ask them more follow-up questions about tobacco chewing, and (b) mothers of low-birthweight babies, looking for a reason, report chewing more completely. Name each bias and give one way to prevent each.
questions.answer: 1. Interviewer bias (information bias arising from the data collector): prevent with a scripted questionnaire asked identically of all, training, and interviewers kept unaware of case status where possible. (b) Recall bias (information bias arising from the participant’s memory): prevent by using exposure recorded before the outcome (antenatal cards), or by choosing controls with another adverse outcome that would prompt similar reflection. Both are differential misclassification, so the direction cannot be assumed.

questions.prompt: Women taking an oral contraceptive visit a doctor more often than other women, and more hypertension is recorded among them. Is this observer bias or detection bias? How would you design the study to prevent it?
questions.answer: Detection bias: the exposure brings women under medical attention, so their blood pressure is measured more often and hypertension is found more often, whatever its true frequency. Observer bias would be a measurer reading blood pressure differently because she knows who takes the pill. Prevention: measure blood pressure in every participant on the same schedule with the same method (equal surveillance), ideally by staff blinded to contraceptive use.

blocks.html: A Catalogue of Named Biases

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The named biases are recurring, recognisable patterns of selection or information bias that arise in particular designs. Each has a mechanism, a usual direction and a design fix. The table below lists those most often met in community medicine research and examinations. Sackett (1979) catalogued the biases of analytic research; the Catalogue of Bias of the Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine, Oxford, gives current definitions.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Memorise the mechanism, not the name. Every row of the table is one of two things: selection that depends on both exposure and outcome (§17.2.1), or a measurement that errs differently in different groups (§17.2.2). If you can say which, you can predict the direction and the fix.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Bias Family Mechanism Usual direction Fix
Berkson’s (admission rate) bias Selection Hospital admission depends on both exposure and disease, so hospital cases and controls are a collider-selected group: “a distortion … which arises because the subjects studied had been admitted to hospital” (Catalogue of Bias) Either way (worked example in §17.2.1: OR 0.33 from a true 1.00) Population controls; incident cases
Neyman (prevalence–incidence) bias Selection Prevalent cases exclude those who died quickly or recovered quickly; if exposure affects survival or duration, exposure among surviving cases is not exposure among all cases Either way; misses exposures that cause rapidly fatal disease “Using incident cases rather than prevalent cases” (Catalogue of Bias)
Healthy-worker effect Selection (some authors: confounding) Employed people are healthier than the general population, because the sick are not hired or leave; “Workers usually exhibit lower overall death rates than the general population” (Last, quoted in Shah, 2009) Towards the null for a harmful exposure when workers are compared with the general population (in Doll’s gas workers, the unexposed had a standardised mortality ratio, recall §7.4.3, of 84) Internal comparison group (exposed vs unexposed workers); exclude the first years of follow-up (Shah, 2009)
Volunteer (self-selection) bias Selection Volunteers differ from others; “Volunteers tend to be more educated, come from high social class” and adhere more (Catalogue of Bias) Volunteers are often healthier and more adherent; biases an association only if volunteering depends on exposure and outcome Random sampling; compare volunteers with non-volunteers on known variables
Non-response bias Selection “Systematic differences between responders and non-responders” (Catalogue of Bias) Unpredictable Repeat visits, short instruments, compare early and late responders; report the response rate
Loss to follow-up (attrition) bias Selection Leaving the cohort or trial depends on exposure and outcome (worked example in §17.2.1) Either way (RR 4.29 from a true 3.54 in §17.2.1) Tracing; intention-to-treat analysis (§15.9); multiple imputation and worst-case sensitivity analysis (§15.4.3, §17.3.1)
Lead-time bias Information (timing of diagnosis) Screening brings diagnosis forward, so survival measured from diagnosis lengthens even if death is not delayed: “overestimating the apparent time surviving with a disease caused by bringing forward the time of its diagnosis” (Catalogue of Bias) Favours screening Compare mortality in randomised screened and unscreened populations, not survival from diagnosis
Length-time bias Selection (by screening) Periodic screening preferentially finds slow-growing disease, which has a better prognosis anyway (Catalogue of Bias) Favours screening Intention-to-screen analysis of all randomised people, including cancers that surface between screens
Overdiagnosis Selection (by screening) Screening finds “cancer” that “would otherwise not go on to cause symptoms or death” (Welch & Black, 2010), inflating incidence and survival Favours screening Randomised trials with mortality end-points and long follow-up
Interviewer bias Information The interviewer asks or records differently according to the participant’s outcome or exposure (§17.2.2) Either way (differential) Scripted neutral questions, training, interviewer blinded to case status
Recall bias Information Cases remember or report past exposure differently from controls (§17.2.2.1) Either way (differential) Records made before the outcome; similar-condition controls
Observer / detection bias Information Assessor’s knowledge of exposure or unequal search for the outcome (§17.2.2.2) Non-blinded assessment exaggerated trial effects on average (Hróbjartsson et al., 2012); detection bias inflated the oestrogen OR (Horwitz & Feinstein, 1978) Blinded assessment; equal surveillance
Hawthorne effect Information (reactivity) People change behaviour “in response to their awareness of being observed” (Catalogue of Bias) Can change the measured behaviour of any observed group; distorts an uncontrolled before–after study A concurrent control group observed in the same way; unobtrusive measures
Immortal-time bias Time-related (misclassified person-time) Follow-up during which, because of how exposure is defined, the outcome could not occur is credited to the exposed (recall §14.6.3; Suissa, 2008) Favours the exposure (spurious protection) Enter exposure that starts after time zero as a time-varying covariate (§14.6.3)

Evidence on the Hawthorne effect is mixed: a systematic review found that most studies reported some effect but that “little can be securely known about the conditions under which they operate, their mechanisms of effects, or their magnitudes” (McCambridge et al., 2014).

blocks.alt: Time line of one patient diagnosed by screening at 55 or by symptoms at 58, dying at 62 either way; survival from diagnosis is 7 years against 4, a lead time of 3 years
blocks.caption: Figure 17.1. Lead-time bias. Screening moves the diagnosis three years earlier; the patient dies at 62 either way, yet “survival” rises from 4 to 7 years.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Lead-time bias with the numbers of Figure 17.1.

  1. Screen-detected: survival = 62 − 55 = 7 years. Symptom-detected: survival = 62 − 58 = 4 years.
  2. Lead time = 58 − 55 = 3 years, exactly the difference in survival.
  3. Age at death is 62 in both. Screening has changed the start of the clock, not the end.

Result: comparing survival from diagnosis rewards screening even when it achieves nothing. Comparing death rates in populations randomised to screening or not removes the problem, because the clock no longer starts at diagnosis.

Bradford Hill’s viewpoints on causation

When chance, bias and confounding have been considered and an association remains, how strong is the case for cause? Recall §11.5: Hill (1965) listed nine viewpoints “from all of which we should study association before we cry causation”. He called them viewpoints, not criteria, and wrote that “None of my nine viewpoints can bring indisputable evidence for or against the cause-and-effect hypothesis and none can be required as a sine qua non” (Hill, 1965).

Viewpoint Hill’s words (Hill, 1965) What it adds Its limit
Strength “First upon my list, I would put the strength of the association.” A large RR is harder to explain away by bias or unmeasured confounding (§17.3.1 quantifies this with the E-value, the confounder strength needed to explain an association away) Weak associations can be causal
Consistency “the consistency of the observed association” Repeated in different places, people and designs Studies can share the same bias
Specificity “the specificity of the association” One exposure, one disease “We must not, however, over-emphasise the importance of the characteristic”: tobacco causes many diseases
Temporality “which is the cart and which the horse?” The cause must come first The only viewpoint that is logically necessary
Biological gradient “biological gradient, or dose-response curve” Risk rises with dose (recall the trend test, §10.6.5) Thresholds exist; a confounder can also have a gradient
Plausibility “It will be helpful if the causation we suspect is biologically plausible.” A mechanism “What is biologically plausible depends upon the biological knowledge of the day.”
Coherence “should not seriously conflict with the generally known facts of the natural history and biology of the disease” Fits what is known Knowledge changes
Experiment “it is possible to appeal to experimental, or semi-experimental, evidence” Removing the exposure reduces the disease Often impossible or unethical
Analogy “it would be fair to judge by analogy” A similar exposure is known to cause a similar effect Analogies are easy to find, so it adds little on its own

points.html: For any named bias, say whether it is selection (depends on both exposure and outcome) or information (differential or non-differential), then predict the direction.
Screening evaluations face three biases that all favour screening (lead time, length time, overdiagnosis). Only a randomised comparison of mortality avoids all three.
Hill’s viewpoints are aids to judgement, not a checklist to score. Only temporality is indispensable.

questions.prompt: Name the bias in each: (a) a study of coal miners finds their all-cause mortality lower than the state’s; (b) a case-control study of tuberculosis and diabetes recruits cases from patients currently on treatment at a DOTS centre; (c) a free cancer screening camp finds that participants have lower cancer mortality than the district; (d) women in a diet study eat more vegetables in the weeks they know they are being observed.
questions.answer: 1. Healthy-worker effect: miners were fit enough to be hired and to stay employed; compare exposed with less-exposed miners instead. (b) Neyman (prevalence–incidence) bias: prevalent cases on treatment exclude those who died early; if diabetes raises early TB mortality, diabetic cases are under-represented and the association is understated. Use newly diagnosed (incident) cases. (c) Volunteer (self-selection) bias: people who attend screening camps are often healthier and more health-conscious; a randomised comparison of invited and not-invited populations is needed. (Lead-time and length-time bias also threaten survival comparisons here.) (d) Hawthorne effect.

questions.prompt: An oral cancer screening programme detects a cancer at age 52 that would have caused symptoms at 55; the patient dies at 58. Compute survival from diagnosis with and without screening and the lead time. What outcome measure should the programme’s evaluation use?
questions.answer:
1. With screening: 58 − 52 = 6 years.
  2. Without screening: 58 − 55 = 3 years.
  3. Lead time = 55 − 52 = 3 years, the whole apparent gain; age at death is 58 either way.

Evaluate by oral-cancer mortality (deaths per 100,000 per year) in populations randomised to screening or not, not by survival from diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Which of Hill’s viewpoints is logically necessary for any causal claim, and why would a lack of specificity be a weak argument against tobacco as a cause of lung cancer?
questions.answer: Temporality: a cause must come before its effect; the other eight add weight but none is required. Specificity (one cause, one effect) is weak because many exposures cause several diseases: tobacco causes lung cancer, oral cancer, heart disease and more. Hill himself warned: “We must not, however, over-emphasise the importance of the characteristic.”
